title: The Reynolds Equation
subtitle: How a thin film of oil carries a load
subject: Tribology

glossary.viscosity: A fluid's resistance to shear, written $\mu$ (Pa·s). Thicker oils have higher viscosity.
glossary.film thickness: The gap $h$ between the two surfaces, filled with lubricant. In real bearings it is a few micrometres.
glossary.hydrodynamic lubrication: Lubrication where the surfaces' own motion drags oil into the gap and builds enough pressure to keep them fully apart.
glossary.Newtonian: A fluid whose shear stress is proportional to shear rate: $\tau = \mu \, du/dy$. Most mineral oils behave this way at moderate shear.
glossary.laminar: Smooth flow in parallel layers, with no turbulent mixing.
glossary.no-slip: The fluid touching a surface moves at exactly that surface's speed.
glossary.Reynolds number: The ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flow. For thin films the useful version is the modified Reynolds number $Re^* = \dfrac{\rho U h}{\mu}\cdot\dfrac{h}{L}$.
glossary.Couette flow: Flow driven by a moving surface dragging the fluid along. Its velocity profile across the film is a straight line.
glossary.Poiseuille flow: Flow driven by a pressure difference. Its velocity profile across the film is a parabola.
glossary.wedge effect: When the gap narrows in the direction of motion, more oil is dragged in than can leave by shear alone, so pressure rises to push the excess back.
glossary.squeeze film: Pressure created when two surfaces approach each other and push the lubricant out of the gap. It appears as the $\partial h / \partial t$ term.

slides.title: The Reynolds Equation
slides.subtitle: How a thin film of oil carries a load
slides.notes: Hover any underlined term for its definition.

slides.title: Why film thickness matters

elements.content: Load capacity scales with [[viscosity]] and falls fast as $h$ grows: $W \propto \mu / h^2$.

- Halve the [[film thickness]] and the same bearing carries about **four times** the load.
- Double the viscosity and the load capacity doubles too.
- This deck's reference film is $h$ = {{h}} µm, thinner than a human hair by a factor of about 15.

slides.notes: The inverse-square dependence on h is the headline result the rest of the deck explains.

elements.content: Thin-film assumptions, two kinds of flow, and conservation of mass.

- The film is thin: $h \ll L$, so pressure is constant across it.
- The lubricant is [[Newtonian]] with constant $\mu$.
- The flow is [[laminar]] and [[no-slip]] holds at both walls.
- Inertia and gravity are negligible next to viscous forces.

*Why inertia drops out.* In a thin film the modified [[Reynolds number]] is tiny, typically far below 1:

$$Re^* = \frac{\rho U h}{\mu}\cdot\frac{h}{L} \ll 1$$

Osborne Reynolds used exactly this argument in 1886^[His paper explained Beauchamp Tower's 1883 experiments, in which oil pressure in a railway journal bearing pushed a plug out of an oil hole.].

slides.title: Two ways oil moves through the gap

elements.content:
The lower surface slides at speed $U$. The flow rate per unit width, $q$, adds a shear-driven [[Couette flow]] and a pressure-driven [[Poiseuille flow]]:

$$q \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{U h}{2}}_{\text{shear}} \;-\; \underbrace{\frac{h^3}{12\,\mu}\,\frac{dp}{dx}}_{\text{pressure}}$$

Pressure pushes oil from high to low $p$, which is why the second term carries a minus sign.

slides.title: The Reynolds equation in one dimension

elements.content: Mass conservation says $dq/dx = 0$. Substituting the flow rate gives one equation for the pressure $p(x)$ in a film of known shape $h(x)$.

**Left side:** how pressure gradients redistribute oil. The $h^3$ factor means a thin film strongly resists being squeezed through.

**Right side:** the source of pressure. It is driven by sliding speed $U$, [[viscosity]] $\mu$, and the slope of the gap $dh/dx$.

If the surfaces are parallel, $dh/dx = 0$ and the right side vanishes: **no pressure builds** and nothing holds the surfaces apart.

A gap that narrows in the direction of motion creates the [[wedge effect]]. That is why bearing pads tilt and journal bearings run off-centre.

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(\frac{\rho h^3}{12\mu}\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left(\frac{\rho h^3}{12\mu}\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\right) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(\rho h\,\frac{U_1 + U_2}{2}\right) + \frac{\partial (\rho h)}{\partial t}$$
Two directions, compressible lubricant (density $\rho$), both surfaces moving, plus a [[squeeze film]] term for surfaces that approach each other.

1. The Reynolds equation is mass conservation for a thin, viscous film.
2. Pressure only builds when the gap changes shape: a wedge, or surfaces squeezing together.
3. Load capacity grows with $\mu U$ and falls roughly as $1/h^2$.
4. Solve it for $p(x, y)$, then integrate $p$ over the pad to get the load $W$.
